summary: A 1970 note commenting on RFC 33 and RFC 36, the host-to-host protocol proposals. It updates RFC 36 and offers feedback from its authors.

eli5.summary: More feedback on the proposed rules for how computers should talk to each other.

subtitle: SDC suggests simplifying reconnection, splitting CLOSE in two, and settling padding, echoing and a common code.

tldr.problem: The proposed Host-to-Host protocol in RFC 33 and RFC 36 left some ambiguities and some costly features, such as reconnection to foreign sockets and a CLOSE command doing two jobs.
tldr.mechanism: The authors propose a local-only SWITCH call, separate BLOCK and CLOSE commands, link numbers instead of foreign socket numbers in commands, and a list of issues to decide.
tldr.outcome: They also state preferences: Hosts avoid double padding by shifting message leaders, no echoing, and a Network Common Code starting from ASCII-8.

today: RFC 44 updates RFC 36 and has not been obsoleted. It is an early discussion document, with status Unknown, so the proposals in it were suggestions rather than a standard.

sections.title: Comments on Reconnection and Closing
sections.content:
A. Shoshani, R. Long and A. Landsberg of System Development Corporation write on 10 April 1970 that they are generally satisfied with the suggestions for the new Host-to-Host protocol, but that a few refinements may help.

They split reconnection into two cases: switching from one local socket to another local socket, which RFC 33 called a "switch", and reconnecting to a socket in a foreign Host. Case 1 is necessary and simple. Case 2 is of doubtful use and needs an elaborate set of commands, since four out of nine commands in RFC 36 handle it. They suggest leaving Case 2 out at first and adding a system call, SWITCH <socket 1> <socket 2>.

They also find that CLOSE in RFC 36 is used both to block a connection and to abort one, so they propose two commands, BLOCK and CLOSE. Both can be acknowledged with the SUSPEND command.
sections.eli5: Switching between your own doors is easy and useful, but switching to someone else's house is hard, so skip that for now. Also, one button should not do two different jobs.

sections.title: Link Numbers and Ports
sections.content:
Once a connection exists, there is no need to keep the foreign socket in the local connection table. Because a link number of the foreign Host corresponds one-to-one with a foreign socket number, commands other than the RFC command can use link numbers. That removes a 40-bit foreign socket number from every entry, which matters because table size is critical for some Hosts. If connections are multiplexed over links, as suggested in RFC 38, the foreign socket would be needed again.

On the term PORT, introduced in RFC 33: if a port maps one-to-one to a socket, ports are redundant. A Host that multiplexes ports over connections would need an additional mechanism.

The initial system calls they list are INITIATE, ACCEPT, SWITCH, LISTEN, CLOSE and TRANSMIT. The commands are commands 0, 1, 3 and 4 of RFC 36 plus BLK <link> and CLS <link>.
sections.eli5: If you already have a numbered lane to your friend, you do not need to write out their long name every time. Just use the lane number.

sections.title: Open Issues from the UCLA Meeting
sections.content:
Three issues raised at the UCLA meeting on March 17, 1970 were put aside, and the authors want them decided with the first version of the protocol, perhaps by setting a date for people to state preferences.

  • Double padding: when a message does not end on a word boundary, either Hosts add their padding on top of the IMP's padding, or Hosts shift messages so they end on a word boundary and adjust the marking.
  • Echoing: echoing, no echoing, or optional echoing, possibly using a bit in the Leader.
  • Code conversion: BB&N first suggested converting in the IMPs using ASCII-8 as the common code. That was rejected because ASCII-8 may be too small for uses such as graphics and conversion may slow the IMPs and use space meant for buffers.

The authors favour a Network Common Code (NCC) using all 256 characters of an 8-bit code, with a "no translation" option for binary data.
sections.eli5: There were three leftover arguments: how to fill empty space at the end of a message, whether to repeat typed letters back, and which shared alphabet to use.

sections.title: The Authors' Preferences
sections.content:
For double padding, they prefer solution V.1.b: it is easy for them to shift the leader of a message rather than the data, so messages go out on a word boundary.

For echoing, they prefer no echoing, because character echoing should be managed locally. For code conversion, they prefer a Network Common Code, where ASCII-8 can be used initially and then expanded according to the needs of the network.
sections.eli5: They end by picking their favourite answer to each leftover argument.

references.text: NWG/RFC 38, suggestion to multiplex connections over links.
